Inua Jamii means “lift the community.”

Lifting communities, one family at a time.

Inua Jamii Foundation walks alongside families facing hunger, illness, school drop-out and unemployment. We give urgent help today, then work with each family and community to build the skills, services and savings that keep them stable tomorrow.

Led by the community we serve

Inua Jamii means “lift the community.” Local people shape every programme, from where we work to how we measure success. Our team lives where we work, our volunteers are neighbours, and families help decide what support they need. That is how change stays after we leave.

How we help

Poverty is never one problem, so our support is never one service. Five focus areas work together around each family.

Food and nutrition

Emergency food parcels, school meals and nutrition lessons so that no child learns or grows on an empty stomach.

Health and wellbeing

Education

Livelihoods

Clean water and shelter

About us

Who we are, why we exist and how we work with the families and communities we serve.

Our story

Inua Jamii Foundation began when neighbours decided not to wait for help from outside. They pooled what they had to feed hungry families and to keep children in school when fees became too much.

As more families came forward, the group became an organisation. We opened a school, started health outreach and set up training for adults who wanted to earn a living. Each step followed the same rule: listen first, then act together.

Today we support thousands of people every year across five focus areas. Many people who once received help now volunteer, teach and lead our programmes.

Mission

To help people in need meet their basic needs and build the skills and confidence to support themselves.

Vision

A community where every person can live in dignity and no family is left behind.

What we value

These principles guide how we treat people, spend money and make decisions.

Dignity

We treat everyone as a partner with strengths, and we ask before we act.

Accountability

We report openly on how funds are used and what they achieve.

Collaboration

We work with local leaders, schools, clinics and other organisations.

Compassion

We respond to need with care and without judgement.

Local leadership

We hire locally and let community members guide our priorities.

Sustainability

We favour skills, savings and services that last beyond a project.

How we work

Every programme follows the same three steps.

Listen

We hold community meetings and home visits to understand each family’s needs before we plan anything.

Act together

Families, volunteers and our team share the work, and everyone has a clear role.

Learn and report

We track results, ask families what worked and share our findings with donors and the community.

Accountability

Donors and families should know that their trust is well placed. We keep our governance simple and open.

  • A board of trustees that meets regularly and reviews our budget and results
  • An annual independent audit and a published annual report
  • A child safeguarding policy that every staff member and volunteer signs
  • A complaints process that families can use without fear

Our journey

  • Year oneNeighbours organise the first food drive and a fund for school fees.
  • Year threeWe register as a foundation and open our first school support programme.
  • Year fiveHealth outreach and livelihood training begin, and Inua Jamii School opens.
  • TodayThousands of people reached every year across five focus areas.

Our work

Five programmes that work together to meet urgent needs and build long-term stability.

Families rarely face just one problem. A child who is hungry cannot learn, and a parent who is ill cannot work. We support the whole family through five connected programmes, and we plan each one with the people it serves.

Food and nutrition

No child learns or grows well on an empty stomach. We provide emergency food and help families eat better for longer.

  • Monthly food parcels for families in crisis
  • School feeding for children
  • Nutrition lessons and kitchen gardens for parents
  • Referrals for children showing signs of malnutrition

Result: Fewer missed school days and healthier children.

Health and wellbeing

We bring basic care closer to people who cannot afford to travel or pay for it.

  • Community health days and screenings
  • Health education on hygiene, maternal and child health
  • Counselling and support groups for young people
  • Referrals and help with medical costs

Result: Illness is caught earlier and families know where to go for help.

Education

Education is the surest way out of poverty. We remove the costs that keep children out of class and support them once they are there.

  • School fees, uniforms and learning materials
  • Mentoring and catch-up classes
  • Support for young mothers to return to school
  • Sponsorship at Inua Jamii School

Result: More children enrolled, attending and finishing school.

Livelihoods

We help adults earn a steady income so that families can support themselves.

  • Skills training in trades, tailoring and business
  • Savings groups and small start-up grants
  • Mentoring for new entrepreneurs
  • Links to markets and employers

Result: Parents earn regularly and rely less on emergency help.

Clean water and shelter

Safe water and a secure home protect health and dignity.

  • Water points and water-storage support
  • Sanitation facilities for homes and schools
  • Repairs for unsafe roofs, floors and doors
  • Hygiene kits during outbreaks and the rainy season

Result: Fewer water-borne illnesses and safer homes.

Who we help

We support families living in poverty in our community, with priority for children, young mothers, older people and people living with disabilities.

Referrals come from schools, clinics, churches and community leaders, and families can also ask us directly. We visit every family before we decide how to help.

Inua Jamii School

Quality learning in a safe, caring place, so every child can reach their potential.

A school built by and for the community

Inua Jamii School is the Foundation’s own school. It gives children from families in need a safe place to learn, grow and discover what they can do.

Fees are kept low, and sponsorship covers children whose families cannot pay, so no child is turned away because of money.

Parents are partners. They meet teachers every term, volunteer at events and help decide how the school grows.

From a market stall to a small shop

Livelihoods · Posted September 2026 · Completed August 2026

Three years ago, a mother of two sold vegetables and handmade beadwork from a small table at the edge of the market. Some days she earned just enough to buy food for her children, and on others she went home with unsold goods and no plan for tomorrow. When she heard about our livelihoods programme, she joined a six-month business course and a savings group of twelve women from her neighbourhood. Together they learned how to keep simple records, how to price their work fairly, and how to save a little every week so that one bad day no longer meant a hungry night.

With her first start-up grant she rented a small shop stall and began stocking grains and household goods alongside her vegetables and beadwork. Her mentor visits every month to review her records and plan for the season ahead. This year the savings group made the traditional outfits for a community celebration, and members performed in them in front of hundreds of neighbours, bringing in new orders for the whole group. Today her business supports her family, and she has hired a young assistant from the same community. She says the biggest change is confidence, because she now knows where her money goes and what she is working towards.

A clinic within walking distance

Health · Posted October 2026 · Completed September 2026

For many families in the area, the nearest clinic was more than an hour away, and the cost of transport alone kept people from seeking care until an illness became serious. Our monthly community health day changed that. Nurses and volunteers set up in the local hall, offering blood pressure checks, child growth monitoring, health talks and advice on nutrition and hygiene, all free of charge. Last month more than a hundred people attended, many for the first time, and those who needed further care were referred to a partner clinic. Our team followed up by phone to make sure they arrived.

The programme has begun to reach people well beyond the hall. Two members of our team were invited onto a local television programme to explain how the health day works and why early check-ups matter, and the response from viewers was immediate, with new families asking where and when to come. Parents tell us the biggest difference is peace of mind, because small problems are now caught early instead of becoming emergencies. We plan to run the health day twice a month and to train more community health volunteers so that care stays close to home.

Back in class after two years

Education · Posted November 2026 · Completed October 2026

After her parents lost their income, a thirteen-year-old girl had to leave school because the family could no longer pay fees. For two years she helped at home and watched her friends move up a grade, all the while keeping her old exercise books and reading them whenever she could. When our team visited the family, we agreed on a plan: a sponsor would cover fees, uniform and books, and a volunteer tutor would meet her twice a week to help her catch up on the lessons she had missed.

She returned to class at the start of this term in a new uniform and with a bag full of books. Her teacher reports that she has already caught up in reading and is now one of the most enthusiastic members of the class, often staying behind to review her notes with classmates. She hopes to become a nurse one day. Her story reminds us that a small amount of support, given at the right moment, can put a whole future back on track.
